page4_img_1.png.title: Callout: Hire a release engineer early
page4_img_1.png.description: A beige rectangular callout contains large, centered blue type reading: “A company needs to get a release engineer on board in the early stage, not the later stage.” The graphic is a typographic pull-quote highlighting a key recommendation from the roundtable (notably voiced by Kim Moir) that release-engineering expertise should be introduced early to set up pipelines, automation, and integration practices. It visually underscores the article’s point that involving release engineers sooner helps avoid last‑minute integration, testing, and deployment problems.

page6_img_1.png.title: Callout: Release engineers are hard to find
page6_img_1.png.description: A large beige callout box with bold blue text stating that release engineers are hard to find because their skill set isn’t taught in school. This graphic highlights a recurring theme from the roundtable: practitioners report a shortage of release engineers and criticize computer-science curricula for emphasizing theory over hands-on skills. The article links this claim to concrete gaps—version control, continuous integration and delivery, release-pipeline tooling, and large-scale systems debugging—that interviewees say make hireable release engineers rare and motivate changes in education and training.

page2_img_1.png.title: Pull quote emphasizing canarying for web releases
page2_img_1.png.description: A large, stylized callout emphasizing that canary deployments are essential for Web services and servers. In the article this highlights the practice of gradually exposing a new build to a subset of users while collecting separate logs and monitoring core metrics (for example, time‑to‑interaction, error rates, and new production errors) to detect regressions. Canarying is described as a key safety step that informs whether to promote a candidate to wider rollout, block it, or take corrective action before full production exposure.

page3_img_pullquote_1.png.title: Pull quote: Mobile deployments are more challenging than Web deployments
page3_img_pullquote_1.png.description: A large, centered pull quote in blue type on a pale background reads that "Mobile deployments are more challenging than Web deployments because we don't own the ecosystem." The image highlights the roundtable participants’ point that app-store/platform control (Apple/Google) limits release engineers’ options: they cannot run fine-grained canaries or push updates on demand, must monitor big canaries for crash rates, cold/warm starts and app size, and often lose users if they require manual re-downloads. It contrasts with Web services, where teams typically own the deployment environment and can use rapid continuous deployment and smaller canary rollouts.

page1_img_1.png.title: Blue header with robotic bird, mechanical hand, and article title
page1_img_1.png.description: A blue-tinted header image that fills the left two-thirds of the page and is overlaid with the article title and author names on the right. The artwork shows a mechanical/robotic bird in flight near the center-left and several articulated robotic-finger assemblies and other machinery at the lower left, with a faint building silhouette in the background. Large white serif title text (the article name and subtitle) and a block of author credit text appear on the right over the blue overlay. The visual serves as a decorative, technology-themed banner for the roundtable on release engineering, emphasizing automation and mechanical systems.
